title: Seeing the tracks
hookLine: second picture: he finds the ox's footprints in the teachings

lines: NOT THE ANIMAL, BUT PROOF IT'S REAL.
cards: A muddy riverbank keeps a footprint for a while. Farmers learn to read those marks, and so does anyone who has lost a dog in the woods: how deep the print sinks, which way the toes point, how fresh the edges look.

A print is not the animal. But it tells you the animal is real, that it came this way, and that you're not chasing a rumor. In the second oxherding picture, the herdsman looks down and sees prints in the mud.

teach.b: First, where the tracks are. The short preface says the herdsman finds them through the sutras and the teachings. He reads, he asks, he listens to people who have walked this way, and something starts to make sense.
That's the footprint: not the ox, but real evidence that there is an ox.

teach.h: A TRACK IS NOT THE OX.
teach.b: Second, a track is not the ox. He has found traces, the preface says, but he has not yet entered the gate. He can talk about the ox, even explain its prints well to someone else.
An old Buddhist image says it another way: a finger pointing at the moon. The teaching points; the trap is staring at the finger.

teach.h: STILL A REAL STEP: A DIRECTION.
teach.b: Third, it still counts as a step. In the first picture there were no prints at all. Now there's a direction.
The verse says, in paraphrase, that the prints are scattered along the stream and under the trees, and however far the ox wanders into the hills, its nose reaches the sky; it can't be hidden.
Fourth, tracks on an ordinary day. A line from a talk stays with you for a week. A friend meets bad news with a steadiness that's hard to explain.
A few quiet minutes in the morning change the afternoon. None of these is awakening. Each is a print in the mud, a sign the way is real and runs somewhere.
The herdsman hasn't arrived, and he isn't making it up.

how: Zen teachers often use the oxherding pictures in talks and retreats as a map of practice, and students reflect on which picture describes where they are; the second picture is commonly read as learning about the way through study.

o: finding real signs of the way, though not the way itself
copying a teacher's footsteps exactly, one by one
proof that the long search is finally over and done

games.q: seeing the tracks: tap the pairs.
p: found in the sutras and teachings
he has traces, not the ox
a finger pointing at the moon
no prints at all, just searching

s: in the second picture, the herdsman has found the ox
he has found only its tracks; the preface says he has not yet entered the gate.
the tracks are found through the teachings
the preface says he comes to understand something through the sutras and teachings.
the picture treats study as worthless
the tracks are real evidence and give him a direction; they just aren't the ox.

games.q: you're the herdsman. you've found prints by the river and can describe them perfectly. what does the second picture say about where you are?
o: you've found traces, but haven't entered the gate.
the prints are a distraction; ignore them.
games.why: the preface says he has found the traces but not yet entered the gate. the tracks are real, and they point onward.

practice: Look back over the last few weeks for one track: a moment, a line, a person, a small habit that seemed to point somewhere. A small print is still a print, so don't weigh whether it's big enough.
Rest your attention on it, the way the herdsman crouches by the mud, and notice which way it points.

wordCard.voice: Seeing the tracks. The second oxherding picture: signs of the ox found in the teachings, real evidence, but not yet the ox itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (jianji): 'seeing the traces', the name of the second oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: the tracks. A track isn't an arrival, but it is real. See you tomorrow, by the riverbank.
